Issued at 1132 PM CST Wed Nov 11 2026

The cold front that passed yesterday was very weak and barely
affected temperatures. The next shortwave trough heading
southward out of Canada will bring cool surface high pressure
with it, resulting in cooler temperatures for Friday and
Saturday, with highs in the 50s both days. A hard freeze is not
expected Friday morning given the moderate air mass and
relatively high dewpoints; but some locations will drop below
freezing. Even on Saturday as the high pressure system passes to
the east, recirculated air from the southeasterly upslope flow 
around the high will keep temperatures on the cool side,
especially given an increase in mid to high level cloud and
afternoon rain. Rain will develop Saturday afternoon across 
southwest Kansas and then spread eastward overnight and into 
Sunday morning as an upper level storm system closes off and 
progresses across Oklahoma. Areas of central Kansas from Larned 
to Hays will receive less rain than areas along the Oklahoma 
state line. Isentropic lift and evaporative cooling Saturday 
night, along with continued upslope winds and low cloud on 
Sunday, will keep thick low cloud and cool temperatures in 
place. Any light rain will end during the morning Sunday, with 
temperatures starting out in the upper 30s to near 40 and rising
only slightly into the lower to mid 40s in the afternoon. Some 
locations along I-70 could warm to 50 degrees if the sun comes 
out; but this is doubtful.

With regard to rain amounts over the weekend, the various
ensemble means continue to show light amounts of .10 to .25"
for locations northwest of Dodge City including Garden City,
Scott City and Ness City, with even lesser amounts at WaKeeney,
Hays and Rush Center. Higher amounts of up to .5" are depicted 
along the Oklahoma state line from Liberal to Coldwater. Given
the lack of potential instability, either elevated or surface
based, heavy rain totals of over 1" are highly unlikely 
anywhere across southwest Kansas. The grand ensemble indicates
10% chances or less of rains over 1" along the Oklahoma state
line. 
 
The next upper level trough is advertised to progress across
the central plains in a weakened state on Wednesday, with
southwest Kansas in the warm sector. Having been suppressed 
into the tropics by the previous system, low level moisture will
be lacking so that any convective instability should be 
minimal. Additionally, the advertised south winds will not be 
enough to scour out the low level cool air; and this will 
enhance the stability. In fact, low clouds could persist through
Monday and Tuesday and maybe even through Wednesday morning
(with perhaps some afternoon sunny breaks), and this would slow
any warm up. Expect highs in the 50s at best, with breezy south
winds making it feel cooler. Even on Wednesday as the upper 
level trough approaches the plains, temperatures may stay on 
the cool side given the moist advection into the cool air mass. 
Even though the days are expected to be chilly with temperatures 
below climatological averages, the nights will feature above 
climatological readings given probable cloud cover, persistent 
south winds and the resultant lack of radiational cooling.

Yet another storm system is advertised to develop across the
western United States by late next week, with a low to mid level
thermal gradient across the central plains. The location of this
front is highly uncertain, as well as the evolution of the upper
level trough. If the front is farther south then a continuation
of a cool pattern (at least for daytime highs) would persist.
However, if the front is north of Kansas, then downslope flow
might propel daytime temperatures into the 60s. It is too early
to tell if precipitation will accompany the late week storm
system.
